paragraphs.text: Every subject of piety aims at the correction of our souls. All the teachings of piety look to this: the salvation of our souls. This is what the word of God works at, what the law of Moses lays down, what the spiritual tongues of the prophets proclaim, and what the apostles cry out for with mouths that are never silent. Everything is for us and because of us, so that our lives may hasten toward correction and be found worthy of piety. Every holy book, then, starts from our salvation, as I have just said. But this book of creation is the beginning, the source and the power of everything in the Law and the Prophets. A house cannot stand without a foundation laid beneath it, and in the same way the beauties of creation cannot shine out unless the beginning of creation is first grasped. I know that many of the holy fathers have gone into the account of creation and said many great and glorious things, as the grace of the Holy Spirit measured out to them. Yet though many great and wonderful things have been said before, nothing prevents us from saying our own part too, as the grace of the Holy Spirit supplies. Those before us were not hindered by those who came before them, and neither are we hindered by those before our generation. For them, for us and for those before them, there is one and the same grace that supplies the power of the Holy Spirit. As Scripture says, "One and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one individually as he wills." So what the fathers said is not thrown out; rather, what we say is set beside it. Even if their words are great and ours small, ours are still built in together with theirs. Suppose a large stone, shaped like a cube, has been set into a building and is shaking slightly: a small stone slipped under it will steady it. In the same way the sayings of the fathers, when they receive small additions, make the building of the church greater. I ask you, my beloved, to pay attention to the ideas in what is said, asking not whether they are unfamiliar but whether they are true. What is customary is not always true, and what is unfamiliar is not always false; in every case one must ask whether what is said is truth or falsehood. I ask you neither to accept the words without examination, as a favour to a friend, nor to throw the argument out as an enemy because it sounds strange, but in every case to see whether truth is the judge of what is said.

"In the beginning," it says, "God made the heaven and the earth." This narrative is a composition of Moses the lawgiver and a revelation of the Holy Spirit. It contains a creation that came about by the power of God and was revealed to Moses by prophetic grace. Moses did not say these things as a historian but as a prophet. He told of what he had not seen, and narrated things of which he had not been a spectator. We once said that there are three kinds of prophecy: the first is by speech, the second by deed, and the third by deed and word together. In the same way there are also three divisions of prophecy here: prophecy about things present, prophecy about things to come, and prophecy about things past. For example, a prophet—Isaiah, let us say—was not present at the events of Moses' time; but since the Spirit of Moses was in him, revealing to him what had happened, it was prophecy. Again, there is prophecy about things present too: someone stands before the prophet and wants to hide something in his mind, and the prophet exposes him, as Elisha did Gehazi, foretelling what is to come and showing what is hidden. Moses told what had happened before, others what was to come. So we must attend to this narrative not as a mere story but as true prophecy spoken by the Holy Spirit. What, then, is the prophet's purpose? Moses set out to do two things: to expound teaching and to sketch out legislation. Though he was a lawgiver, he did not begin with legislation but with creation. Why did he want first to show God as the creator and master of all? So that God would be shown to be giving laws not to strangers but to his own. If he had not first shown him to be the creator of the world, he would not have been shown to be a credible lawgiver for the world. To give laws to those who belong to another is violence; to instruct one's own follows naturally. In the same way John the evangelist did not set out Christ's legislation until he had declared his lordship, saying: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being that has come into being. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." Once he had called him maker and creator, he then introduces him as teacher and lawgiver of all. Moses had another purpose as well. Why did blessed Moses mention heaven, earth, sea, waters and what comes from them, yet make no mention of angels, archangels, seraphim or cherubim? Because he was fitting his legislation to the times. He knew whom he was addressing: people who had come out of Egypt, who had learned the Egyptian error, who worshipped the things of heaven and earth—sun, moon and stars, rivers, springs and waters. So he passed over the creation of invisible things and poured out his discourse on the visible ones, to persuade those who worshipped them not to think them gods but works of God. Nor was it necessary at that time to tell them about angels and archangels, lest he feed their disease again. If they spoke of many gods without seeing angels or any spiritual beings, how much more, had they heard of angels or archangels, would they have thought these to be gods? Instead he mentions heaven and earth, mountains and waters and everything that comes from them, so that through what is seen he might explain the Invisible, and through the works show the Craftsman. The three young men in Babylon did the same. Because they were among that nation which fought against God, where there was no knowledge of God but idols were worshipped, they said while in the furnace: "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord." Why did they not stop there, but go on to name angels, heavens, earth, fire, water, cold, heat and everything of that kind, enumerating creation part by part? So that they might wash the whole of creation, cleanse all that was made, and leave behind no spark of impiety. So too here: Moses, wishing to drive the Egyptian error out of the Jews, mentions heaven and earth as things that came into being, to point to what was made and to call to mind the One who made it: "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth."

Turn your mind to me here. I marvel at how John and Moses had the same opening. Moses says, "In the beginning he made," and John says, "In the beginning was." Yet the one speaks usefully and the other properly. Where creation is concerned, Moses put "made"; where the Creator is concerned, the evangelist put "was." There is a great difference between "made" and "was." The one came to be when it did not exist; the other was, ever existing. "In the beginning he made," and "In the beginning was." Being belongs to God, coming-to-be to creatures, just as the evangelist distinguishes them. Of the Saviour he says: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning. In him was life, and the life was the light of men." Six times he says "was," to express being. But of the servant, when he had proclaimed the One who is and came to the slave, to John, he says: "There came to be a man." God was; but a man came to be. If they dare to say of the Saviour too that he "was" only after coming to be, then he is no different from the earth. Pay attention, I beg you. If the heretic says that Christ "was" after coming to be, and did not exist before he came to be, what advantage does he have over the earth? For Moses said of the earth too: "And the earth was." If, then, they take "in the beginning was" to mean being made, and not to refer to his eternal nature, he has no advantage over the earth. Both God the Word "was" and the earth "was." But there he was in the beginning without having come to be, ever existing; whereas the earth "was" after coming to be. The lawgiver did not first say "and the earth was" until he had said "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth." First "made," and then "was." We know, brothers, that these subtle questions seem hard to the minds of most people. But on a fast day, when our souls are more sober, we ought to discuss the deeper ideas. "In the beginning was" and "In the beginning made." They used the same opening—"in the beginning" and "in the beginning"—to show that there is one root of piety, which both taught the lawgiver and enlightened the theologian. The two covenants are sisters, set down by one Father. That is why they utter their word in harmony. They bear almost the same image and likeness. Just as sisters born of one father share distinctive marks of resemblance, so too, since the two covenants were born of one Father, they bear a strong likeness to each other. Indeed, in the old covenant the Law comes first and the Prophets follow; and in the new grace the Gospel comes first and the apostles follow. There, there are twelve prophets, each of the twelve [?]—the twelve, Hosea and his company—and four: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel. In the new, there are twelve apostles and four evangelists. Again, there God's first calling began with brothers: he took Moses and Aaron as the first heralds. And in the Gospel the first calling is of Peter and Andrew. There the grace was single, here double. There two brothers were called, Moses and Aaron; here a double pair of brothers, Peter and Andrew, James and John. Because the Saviour wished to imprint on us the love that comes from the Holy Spirit, and to make us brothers in disposition and in spirit, he took nature as a foundation, fixed onto it the affections of nature, and on that built the foundation of the church. The first sign in the old covenant was the river turned into blood; the first sign in the new was water turned into wine. But this is not the time to set out the whole resemblance point by point. Let us return to our subject. "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth." In six days God made all things. But the first day differs from those that followed it. On the first day God made things out of what did not exist. From the second day on, God made nothing out of what did not exist, but transformed as he wished what he had made on the first day. As for you who have considered and examined this: if you find it to be true, agree; if you do not find it true, accuse me, and I accept the accusation. For it gives me ample opportunity for a defence.

On the first day, then, God made the materials of created things; on the other days, the shaping and ordering of created things. Let me explain what I mean. He made heaven when it did not exist—not this heaven, but the one above it, for this one came into being on the second day. God made the upper heaven, of which David says: "The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord." This is an upper story. Just as in a two-storied house there is a ceiling in between, so the Lord, building the world like a single house, set this heaven as a middle ceiling, with the waters above it. That is why David says: "He who roofs his upper chambers with waters." So he made heaven when it did not exist, the earth when it did not exist, the abysses when they did not exist, winds, air, fire, water. He made the matter of everything that came into being on the first day. But someone will surely say: "It is written that he made the heaven and the earth, but nothing is written about water, fire and air." First of all, brothers, in saying that heaven and earth came into being, he explained the contents by means of what contains them. When he said, "God made man, taking dust from the earth," he named the creature he formed but did not list its members; he did not say, "God made eyes and ears and a nose." By saying "man" he included all the members. In the same way, by saying "God made the heaven and the earth," he included everything, and brought in along with them the darkness and the abysses as things that had come into being. "Darkness," it says, "was over the abyss." The mass of waters is called the abyss. That the abysses too came into being, Scripture testifies when it says: "Before he made the abysses, before the earth came to be." So the abysses too came into being. Next, hear when the air came into being: "And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters." Here he does not mean the Holy Spirit, for the uncreated is not counted among creation; rather, he calls the motion of the air "spirit." Just as it is written in the account of Elijah the prophet, "And the sky grew dark with cloud and wind (pneuma)," so here too "spirit" means the nature of air. It remains to show where fire came into being. God said, "Let there be light," and the nature of fire came into being. For this fire of ours is not the only fire; the powers above are fire too, and the fire above is akin to the fire here among us. You may ask why the one is quenched and the other is not. Well, God made the angels spirits and our souls spirits, but our souls are in bodies, while the angels are outside bodies. As with souls and angels, so one can see it with fire. The fire above is without matter; the fire below is with matter. The fire above is akin to these, just as our soul is akin to the angels. In the sense that they are spirits, our souls too are spirits, as the three young men say: "Bless him, you spirits and souls of the righteous"; and again: "He who makes his angels spirits." A soul is not seen without a body, nor can fire be seen without tow or brushwood or some other material. That this fire of ours is not foreign to that other fire, creation teaches us. Many people often borrow fire from the sun and kindle with it. If it were foreign, how could something foreign be taken from it? Moreover, there is in heaven a great immaterial fire, such that fire appeared on Mount Sinai too, not with wood laid beneath it; rather, God brought that immaterial fire itself into view. And as one might say that this fire is small beside that great one, so Moses says: "From heaven the Lord made his voice heard, and God showed his great fire," to show that this one is small. All these, then, are fire—lightning, the stars, the sun and the moon—and our own fire is akin to them. See how lightning is related to the stars even in name: lightning (astrapē) and stars (astra). And the Saviour, to show that fire and lightning are akin, says in the Gospel: "The lamp of the body is the eye. If then your eye is full of light, your whole body will be full of light." So says the Saviour. Then he adds: "as when a lamp lights you with its lightning," calling the gleam of the lamp the lamp's "lightning."

So everything came into being: fire came into being, the abysses came into being, the winds, the four elements—earth, fire, water, air. What he left out, Moses sums up, as it were in an unexpected place [?], saying: "In six days God made the heaven and the earth and all that is in them." Just as with the body he did not name all the members, so with creation he did not list everything, even though all things were constructed together with the world. If there were no fire in the earth, people would not today strike fire out of stone or wood; for wood rubbed together produces fire. Now pay close attention. "Darkness," it says, "was over the abyss." Did God make darkness, then, someone asks? We know that the thought is deep. But since we often find ourselves among both those who listen with love and those who like to find fault, we must not leave the matter unexamined, lest the promise be great and the result small. Where, then, does darkness come from? For God, someone says, did not make it; God is the maker neither of darkness nor of gloom. What, then, is darkness? Many have wanted to say that it is the shadow cast by heaven. When the upper heaven came into being, they say, and the lights were left above, the earth was laid bare and darkness came about. But the heaven above is full of light, not dark: even if it had neither sun nor moon nor stars, its very nature was radiant. If, then, heaven lay above and the earth was spread out below, with the source of light above and what is lit below, where does darkness come from? It seems to me that since water lay on the surface of the earth, mist and gloom gathered about the waters, as happens even now over rivers; the mist, raising gloom, made clouds, and the clouds, casting their shadow, made darkness. That a cloud brings on darkness Scripture says: "And the sky grew dark with clouds." We should not be ignorant of the heretics' allegories either. Some heretics have dared to say that the darkness is the devil and the abyss the demons; and when God said, "Let there be light," that means, he said, "Let the Son come into being." And they are not ashamed to call the devil older than the Son. For if the abyss is a demon and the darkness the devil, and after this God said, "Let there be light"—that is, the Son—then the devil is not only of equal rank with him but older. But such impiety does not even deserve mention. The darkness at that time, then, came from the clouds. In the same way there was darkness in Egypt, not because it was night but because a mist had arisen. So it was on Mount Sinai too: there was darkness not because night had fallen but because a cloud cast its shadow. So too the darkness came about at the cross of Christ. We have brought these in so that you may not be ignorant of what is said. It was not that night came on, but that there was shadow and obstruction. So we must not handle the divine oracles carelessly. "And the Spirit of God was borne over the water." He calls the wind "spirit," as he says elsewhere: "With a violent wind (pneuma) you will shatter the ships of Tarshish," calling the movement of the air "spirit." Do not suppose that air is one thing and wind another. Air itself, when set in motion, makes wind, as experience bears witness. We often set still air moving with a fan or a cloth and make wind from the movement of the air. So, to show by means of the word "spirit" that wind is a movement of air, he said "was borne"; for to be borne over creation is the property of wind. God said, "Let there be light." Why did Moses not say that God said, "Let there be heaven," "Let there be sea," but there said "he made" and here "he said"? With us, word comes before deed: we first speak, then act. He wanted to show God acting first, so as to present creation as swifter than any word. When God produces the materials by power, he says "he made"; but when he was about to set all things in order, and light was the beginning of that order, he introduces a fitting word. Again, since the first work of God was light and his last work was man, God first produced light by a word, and later man by a deed, completing his work from light to light.

Hear how light and man are alike. Light shows what exists. Man, the light of the world, came in and showed you the light of skill, the light of knowledge. Light showed the grain; understanding made bread. Light showed the cluster on the vine; the light of understanding showed the wine within the cluster. Light showed wool; the light of man showed a garment. Light showed a mountain; the light of understanding showed a quarry. That is why the Saviour too calls the apostles light, saying: "You are the light of the world." Why does he call them light? Not only to honour them, but also to show the hope of the resurrection. Just as light, when it sets in the evening, is not destroyed but hidden, and once hidden appears again, so man too, sent off to the tomb as to a kind of setting, is kept for the dawn of the resurrection. "Let there be light." He told what came to be, but he did not explain how, nor did he learn it. "That light came into being," he says, "I know; but how it came into being I do not grasp." That is why the Saviour told the apostles: "It is not for you to know times or seasons, which the Father has set by his own authority." If it is not for us to know times or seasons, can the Master of times and the Maker of the ages be grasped by human reasoning? God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. O that holy and great power! O great wonders! Light came into being, and God calls the light day and the darkness night. Why does he call it day (hēmera)? Because everything bright and cheerful is called gentle (hēmeros). That is why we call kindness gentleness, and call tamed beasts gentle. "And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night." Why night? Because by night it brings sleeping man to the remembrance of death, all but saying: "Learn, O man, who you are. You are mortal; you are a slave to sleep. Why do you imagine things beyond you?" For night (nyx) is compunction (katanygē). Hence David also says: "What you say in your hearts, be pierced with compunction for it on your beds." Indeed, at night a man lies neither dead nor alive. Ask a heretic: "What is he—alive or dead?" If he says alive, say: "Then why does he not perceive those who are talking or walking about?" If he says dead, say: "Then how does he breathe?" What breathes is not dead; what does not perceive is not alive. You do not see yourself, yet you imagine things beyond you. But let this suffice for the first day. Evening has overtaken us, as it overtook the events of the first day there, and we have set these things out as best we could, deep as the ideas were. It is for the faithful to search out what has been said and to study the narrative.

But we, who are nurslings of a holy fast and have feasted on heavenly things while our bodies go without food, should be eager to keep the fast holy. For Scripture says, "Sanctify a fast." Do we sanctify it, or are we sanctified by it? The prophet said this in the sense of "keep it holy." When we pray, "Hallowed be your name," we are not praying on behalf of his name, for his name hallows all things. Rather, because his name has been called upon us (we are called Christians after Christ), we say, "May your name be hallowed in us." For with the Holy One all things are holy, and nothing that is not holy draws near to God. God is holy, and he rests among the holy. His heaven too is holy: "He will hear him from his holy heaven." The angels are holy: "When the Son of Man comes in his glory with his holy angels." The land that holds his worship is holy: "And he will seek," it says, "to pervert the covenant upon his holy land." And David says the court is holy: "Worship the Lord in his holy court." Isaiah says the temple is holy: "For your temple is holy, wonderful in righteousness." The dumb sheep that were sacrificed in those days were called holy: "Like holy sheep," it says, "in Jerusalem." The covenant is holy: "And he will strengthen his holy covenant with many." The city itself was called holy: "And upon the holy city of our fathers, Jerusalem." For nothing that is not holy comes to God. That is why Paul says, "And holiness, without which no one will see God." We have fasted from bread; let us fast from injustice too. You do not eat bread? Then do not eat the flesh of the poor, so that God may not say of you as well, "Those who devour my people as they eat bread." You do not drink wine? Then do not let anger make you drunk, so that you may not hear from the Lawgiver, "Their wrath is after the likeness of the serpent," and again, "Their wine is the wrath of dragons." For when you oppress a poor man and he groans, you are found before God eating the bread of tears. That is why God also says, "You covered my altar with tears." So God rebukes those who weep at the altar, and he says, "Priests, go in and weep." But he rebukes them not because they themselves were weeping, but because the wronged, orphans and widows, were pleading there at the altar. And to show that he is speaking of them, he added, "With weeping and wailing and toil." It is worth looking further at our sacrifices. The table set before the soul, then, is the word of God. A body that fasts is sanctified; a soul that is not fed wastes away. May the body fast from sins, and the soul feast on the divine teachings. You cannot eat the bread of Christ and the bread of tears, as Paul says: "You cannot partake of the table of Christ and the table of demons." So the one who fasts must abstain from foods, and first of all from sins. For every day the angels take note of who has resolved to abstain from greed, or fornication, or injustice, or some other sin. These are the fasts that the angels record and God stores up. For just as, brothers, governors report everything to the emperor through their dispatches, so too the angels report to God everything that happens. They are not informing him as though he did not know; they are fulfilling the ministering rank assigned to them in creation. I would ten thousand times sooner call blessed the one who eats than the one who fasts and does wrong. I say this not to abolish fasting but to proclaim godliness. For eating is not evil; sinning is wicked. As God says of a certain righteous man, "Did not your father eat, and do my will?" So also elsewhere: "The fast of the fourth month, and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the tenth shall be for you joy and gladness and good feasts; and love the truth." But the visible light has shone out so that the maker of light may be proclaimed. Evening has come, setting its seal on the day's course. The beginning is good; let the end be added to it. Do not wickedly cast it away, but listen to David: "For the end: Do not destroy." May the God of this light enlighten you all with reason, law, faith, righteousness and self-control, in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom and with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
